intro: You've searched for the best guarantor mortgage near you, so you're likely exploring how a family member can help you qualify for a mortgage or afford a larger loan. A guarantor mortgage involves someone else's income or property being used as security or support for your borrowing. Finding the right broker means looking at who is regulated, what they cover, and how they'll help everyone understand the risks.
need_heading: What people searching for a guarantor mortgage usually need
need_lead: Most people looking for a guarantor mortgage want to know how a relative can help them get on the property ladder or borrow more, and who locally can advise on the options.
needs: You want to buy your first home but your income alone isn't enough for the mortgage you need, so a parent or other family member has offered to act as guarantor.
You're a parent or relative considering using your savings or property to help a family member borrow, and you want to understand what that commitment really means.
You've been told by a lender that you need a guarantor, and you're looking for a broker near you who deals with these mortgages.
You're exploring joint borrower, sole proprietor arrangements where you'd be named on the mortgage but not on the property title, and you need advice on how that works.
You want to compare guarantor mortgage options from different lenders but don't know which brokers near you have access to them.
context_heading: The 'best' and 'near me' parts of your search
context: There's no single best guarantor mortgage or broker, because the right fit depends on your circumstances, the guarantor's situation, and which lenders will accept your case. Instead of looking for a label, check that any broker is authorised by the Financial Conduct Authority (FCA) and appears on the FCA register, and ask whether they search the whole market or a limited panel. That tells you far more than a ranking ever could.

Searching near you makes sense if you'd prefer face-to-face advice, but many brokers work remotely across the UK. What matters most is that the broker understands guarantor mortgages and explains how they're paid, whether by lender commission, a fee, or both. If something goes wrong, you can complain to the firm and then to the Financial Ombudsman Service.
tell_heading: What to tell iComply when you enquire
tell: Say who the guarantor will be, such as a parent or other family member, and whether they're offering savings, property, or income support.
Explain your own situation briefly, including whether you're buying alone or with someone else, and whether you're a first-time buyer.
Mention the type of property and area you're looking at, so the broker knows the kind of mortgage you'll need.
Say whether you're interested in a joint borrower, sole proprietor arrangement or a more traditional guarantor mortgage.
Note any preferences about location, such as whether you want a broker you can visit in person or are happy with phone and online advice.
Include anything that might affect lender choice, like being self-employed or having a small deposit, so the broker can prepare.
questions: Are you authorised by the Financial Conduct Authority, and can you show me your entry on the FCA register?
Do you search the whole of the market or a limited panel of lenders for guarantor mortgages?
How are you paid for arranging a guarantor mortgage, whether by lender commission, a fee, or both?
What are the risks for my guarantor, and will they be advised to seek independent legal advice?
Can you explain how a joint borrower, sole proprietor mortgage works compared with a guarantor mortgage?
What happens if my guarantor's circumstances change, or if I want to remove them from the arrangement later?

faqs.a: A guarantor mortgage lets a family member support your borrowing, often by using their savings or property as security or by agreeing to cover payments if you can't. The guarantor takes on real risk, so they should get independent advice before agreeing.

faqs.q: Do I need a broker near me for a guarantor mortgage?
faqs.a: Not necessarily. Many brokers advise on guarantor mortgages remotely across the UK, so being nearby isn't essential. What matters is that the broker is authorised by the FCA and understands these products.

faqs.q: Can a guarantor be removed from a mortgage later?
faqs.a: It may be possible to remove a guarantor if your circumstances improve and the lender agrees, but this depends on the lender's criteria and your affordability. A broker can explain the options for your situation.

faqs.q: What should my guarantor think about before agreeing?
faqs.a: Your guarantor should consider the risk to their own home or savings, and how their circumstances might change. They should get independent legal advice, and a broker can explain how the arrangement works.

extra_heading: What happens after we introduce you to a broker
extra: Once you've told us what you need, we introduce you to a mortgage broker who deals with guarantor and family-assisted mortgages. They then quote you directly, with the price on application, so you'll know where you stand before committing to anything. The broker will want to understand your income, your deposit, and the guarantor's circumstances before suggesting any lender.

At that first conversation, expect questions about whether the guarantor is offering savings, property, or simply a pledge of support, because lenders treat each differently. The broker should also explain the difference between a guarantor mortgage and a joint borrower, sole proprietor arrangement, since the two carry different responsibilities for the guarantor. Ask them to set out the risks for your guarantor in plain terms, including what happens if you fall behind on payments.

It's also worth asking how the broker is paid, whether by lender commission, a fee, or both, and whether they search the whole market or a limited panel. Because the guarantor is taking on real financial risk, they should be encouraged to get independent legal advice before signing anything. A good broker will welcome those questions rather than brush past them.

extra_faqs.q: Will my guarantor need their own legal advice?
extra_faqs.a: It's strongly advisable. A guarantor is taking on genuine risk, and independent legal advice helps them understand exactly what they're signing up to. Ask the broker whether the lender will require this, as some do.

extra_faqs.q: Can a guarantor mortgage help if I'm self-employed?
extra_faqs.a: It can, because the guarantor's support may strengthen your application where your income is harder for lenders to assess. A broker who deals with guarantor mortgages can explain which lenders are more open to self-employed borrowers in your position.

extra_faqs.q: How is a guarantor mortgage different from a joint mortgage?
extra_faqs.a: With a joint mortgage, everyone named is a borrower and usually owns a share of the property. A guarantor mortgage, or a joint borrower sole proprietor arrangement, lets someone support your borrowing without necessarily being on the title, though their risk is still real.
